stem: Which scenario is a good candidate for the routing workflow pattern: (A) requests that fall into a handful of distinct, identifiable categories each needing different handling, or (B) requests that are all essentially identical in nature?
explanation: Scenario A (distinct, identifiable categories needing different handling) is the good candidate for routing, since the whole value of routing comes from directing different kinds of requests to specialized handling; if all requests are essentially identical (scenario B), there's nothing meaningfully distinct to route between, making a single generalized prompt just as effective.

choices.text: Scenario A; routing's value comes from directing distinct categories to specialized handling.
choices.reasoning: Correct: routing is valuable specifically when there are meaningfully distinct categories that benefit from different handling; without that distinction, a single generalized prompt serves just as well.

choices.text: Scenario B; routing is most valuable when all requests are essentially identical in nature.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this reverses the actual fit; routing's value specifically comes from handling distinct categories differently, which doesn't apply to uniform, identical requests.

choices.text: Neither scenario benefits from routing under any circumstances.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: scenario A is a textbook good fit for routing; the pattern does provide real value in that case.

choices.text: Both scenarios are equally good candidates for routing.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: these two scenarios have meaningfully different characteristics that make one (A) a clearly better fit for routing than the other (B).

stem: A developer wants to measure whether their compaction strategy is actually preserving enough information for the agent to still perform well after compaction occurs. What is a reasonable way to evaluate this?
explanation: Comparing agent task success/quality on runs with compaction enabled versus disabled (or against a longer, uncompacted baseline) on representative long-running tasks is a reasonable, empirical way to evaluate whether the compaction strategy is preserving enough of what actually matters, rather than assuming a given summarization approach works well without any measurement of its actual downstream effect on task performance.
reference: Empirically evaluating compaction's effect on task success

choices.text: Compare agent task success/quality with compaction enabled versus disabled (or a longer uncompacted baseline) on representative long-running tasks.
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is a concrete, empirical evaluation approach that directly measures whether the compaction strategy actually preserves what matters for task success, rather than relying on an untested assumption about summarization quality.

choices.text: There is no way to measure whether a compaction strategy is effective.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: comparing task success with and without (or with more/less aggressive) compaction is a concrete, feasible way to evaluate its effectiveness.

choices.text: Compaction strategies never need evaluation since they are always guaranteed to preserve all necessary information perfectly.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: summarization is inherently lossy, so this assumption is unsound; empirical evaluation is needed to actually verify how well a given strategy preserves what matters.

choices.text: This can only be evaluated by contacting Anthropic support for a manual review of the compaction logic.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is something the developer can and should evaluate directly using their own representative tasks and comparison, without needing outside support.

stem: A developer building an orchestrator-workers system for large-scale content moderation wants each worker to focus on a single piece of content in isolation, without seeing the orchestrator's broader context (e.g. platform-wide trends). Is this scoping choice reasonable?
explanation: Yes, generally reasonable, since scoping each worker to just the specific content it needs to assess reduces its context to what's actually necessary for making a per-item judgment, avoiding unnecessary token cost and potential distraction from irrelevant platform-wide context that isn't needed to evaluate that specific individual piece of content, consistent with the general principle of scoping worker context to just what each sub-task actually requires.
reference: Reasonable per-item worker scoping for moderation

choices.text: Yes, generally reasonable; scoping each worker to just the content it needs to assess.
choices.reasoning: Correct: this reflects the same sound context-scoping principle discussed for orchestrator-workers generally, giving each worker only what it actually needs for its narrow, specific task rather than unnecessary broader context.

choices.text: No; every worker must always have access to the exact same full context as the orchestrator, with no scoping ever being appropriate.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this contradicts the general principle that scoping worker context to just what's needed for its specific sub-task is a sound, cost-efficient design choice, not something to always avoid.

choices.text: This scoping choice is technically impossible; workers always automatically inherit the orchestrator's full context.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: each worker's request is constructed independently, so its context is entirely up to what the application chooses to include, not an automatic inheritance of the orchestrator's full context.

choices.text: This scoping choice has no relationship to cost or performance.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: scoping context appropriately per worker directly affects token cost (less unnecessary content) and can affect quality/focus, making it a relevant, not unrelated, consideration.

stem: A developer describes their system design process as: 'start with the simplest single call; if that's insufficient, try a workflow pattern; if that's still insufficient, consider an agent.' What principle does this progression embody?
explanation: This embodies the principle of incremental complexity, adding architectural sophistication only as actually demonstrated to be necessary by the task's real requirements, rather than starting with the most complex, flexible option (a full agent) by default and only simplifying if forced to, which reflects the broader engineering wisdom of not over-engineering a solution beyond what a problem genuinely requires.

choices.text: Incremental complexity: adding architectural sophistication only as demonstrated necessary by the task's real requirements.
choices.reasoning: Correct: this captures the sound engineering principle of matching solution complexity to actual demonstrated need, avoiding the unnecessary cost, latency, and unpredictability of over-engineering a solution beyond what the task genuinely requires.

choices.text: This progression embodies a principle of always maximizing cost for every system, regardless of actual need.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this progression actually minimizes unnecessary cost/complexity by starting simple and only escalating when genuinely needed, the opposite of maximizing cost by default.

choices.text: This progression has no underlying principle and is simply an arbitrary, unmotivated ordering.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this ordering reflects a deliberate, well-reasoned engineering principle (incremental complexity matched to demonstrated need), not an arbitrary sequence.

choices.text: This progression only applies to tasks involving image content.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the incremental-complexity principle applies broadly to any kind of task, not specifically to image-related ones.
